text: The way i got rid of mine was just to stop over watering. They need moist soil to reproduce so if you just let the plants dry out between watering that will get rid of them for good. Most people who try treatments do not have lasting success because they don't deal with the root cause (pun intended) which is damp soil and/or insufficient drainage. make sure water is not pooling in the bottom of your pot. if you have an indoor pot with no drainage that you have planted into directly, you are going to need to repot. A cheap plastic pot that fits inside the indoor pot will work well. it can be removed for watering and have excess water tipped out. even better if it can be raised off the bottom of the pot with gravel/stones.treat them once to bring numbers down, but long term focus on water and drainage
label: pest_management

text: Fungus gnats. They breed and emerge from damp soil. They’re not the absolute worst plant pest but they can do some serious damage to your roots if they are in high enough numbers. There are some physical barriers you can use along with the sticky traps which will prevent them hatching from the soil and break the breeding cycle. Some people use a thick layer of vermiculite or something similar such as crushed eggshells , shell grit etc , there are also some specialized top dressings available from garden centres that supposedly kill them off without harming the plant. Another option is to repot with fresh, clean potting mix and avoid overwatering

They my friend are fugus gnats.They thrive in damp, dare I say the word l, moist potting mix/soil.They'll be laying eggs under the surface of the top of the soil.These buggers need Eco Neem oil at the recommended dose for potting mix (3ml on 8 litre of potting mix).You'll need to spray and drench the top 5cm to 10cm of soil a couple times to kill them and their yet to be born offspring.I'm having some success with Eco Neem oil.. use sparingly. It's bloody pricey.

text: Honestly, all the tips you'll get to rid your life of fungus gnats will just drive you crazy. Some might work for a short time but there is no permanent solution. Plants simply are not supposed to be grown indoors, so there will always be challenges to keeping them, and fungus gnats are one of them. The best thing you can do it get used to them. After about a year, fresh potting soil will "settle down" and you'll see them far less. All my indoor plants had gnats for about 6 months. I did nothing about them and now I have none. I expect they'll be back one day, then will leave again and the cycle will continue.

text: Gnats are in the potting mix, probably sourced from council dumps. I would suggest either repotting the plant in new potting mix after washing the roots to get rid of residual mix/eggs. Or, putting the potting mix in the oven for awhile to completely kill off any eggs etc. Suggest maybe an hour or so at around 80c
